readings.title: The Cow
readings.challenge: Hear a child thank a cow and then give her advice.
readings.focus: The child thanks the cow for her milk and tells her where to eat, so the milk will stay sweet.
readings.context: Ann and Jane Taylor wrote these rhymes for young children about two hundred years ago. Hemlock is a poisonous weed; rank means growing thick and coarse. Cowslips are yellow wildflowers; to dine is to eat dinner.

excerpt.locator: “The Cow,” the complete poem; opens “Thank you, pretty cow, that made Pleasant milk to soak my bread, Ev’ry day, and ev’ry…”; closes “…bubbling water flows, Where the grass is fresh and fine, Pretty cow, go there and dine.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the child thank the cow?
facilitatorNotes: For the milk that soaks the child’s bread, every day and every night.
evidence: Thank you, pretty cow, that made
Pleasant milk to soak my bread,

questions.prompt: What should the cow not eat, and what should she eat instead?
facilitatorNotes: Not the hemlock on the weedy bank, but the yellow cowslips, which will make her milk sweet.
evidence: Do not chew the hemlock rank,
But the yellow cowslips eat,

questions.prompt: Describe the place where the child tells the cow to go and dine. Why might a good meadow make good milk?
facilitatorNotes: Where violets grow, water bubbles and the grass is fresh and fine. A child who connects good food with good milk is following the poem’s idea.
evidence: Where the bubbling water flows,
Pretty cow, go there and dine.

readings.title: The Sparrows
readings.challenge: Hear a child try to make friends with shy birds.
readings.focus: A child promises the nest-building sparrows that she only wants to watch them, never to cage them.
readings.context: Sparrows are small brown birds that build untidy nests. A jenneting tree is an early apple tree. “Dick” was a pet name for a bird. Read gently, as if not to frighten the birds away.

excerpt.locator: “The Sparrows,” the complete poem; opens “Hop about, pretty sparrows, and pick up the hay, And the twigs, and the wool, and the…”; closes “…be! Then come, pretty bird, while I quietly stand At the foot of the jenneting tree.”.

questions.prompt: What are the sparrows picking up, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Hay, twigs, wool and moss to build their nest, their “house.”
evidence: Hop about, pretty sparrows, and pick up the hay,
How you gather the twigs for your house;

questions.prompt: What does the child promise not to do?
facilitatorNotes: Not to catch them and fasten them in a cage, where they would hop all day on a stick or flutter in a rage.
evidence: I don’t mean to catch you, you dear little Dick,
And fasten you up in a cage;

questions.prompt: What would make the child happiest? Do you think the sparrows will come?
facilitatorNotes: If a sparrow would eat a crumb from her hand. The poem does not say whether one comes; children can guess, perhaps saying she must stand very still.
evidence: Oh dear, if you’d eat a crumb out of my hand,
Then come, pretty bird, while I quietly stand

readings.title: The Spring Nosegay
readings.challenge: Gather the flowers of one season, one by one.
readings.focus: A walk to make a spring posy visits hedge, meadow and garden in turn.
readings.context: A nosegay or posy is a small bunch of flowers. “Prickly May” is hawthorn blossom; to blow means to bloom. Primroses, cowslips, snowdrops and crocuses are early spring flowers. If you can, pick or look at a few flowers together after reading.

excerpt.locator: “The Spring Nosegay,” the complete poem; opens “Come, my love, ’tis pleasant spring, Let us make a posy gay: Ev’ry pretty flow’r we’ll…”; closes “…the garden walk: All these pretty flow’rs we’ll bring, To make a posy for the spring.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker want to make, and when?
facilitatorNotes: A bright posy, in pleasant spring. The speaker asks “my love,” a child or friend, to help.
evidence: Come, my love, ’tis pleasant spring,
Let us make a posy gay:

questions.prompt: Name some flowers that go into the spring posy.
facilitatorNotes: Daisies, May blossom, violets, primroses, cowslips, a buttercup or two, snowdrops and crocuses. Any of these is right.
evidence: Daisy white, and prickly May;
Where the purple violets blow.

questions.prompt: Where do they look for the flowers? Where would you look near your home?
facilitatorNotes: Along the hedge, in the meadows and up and down the garden walk. Children can name places near them.
evidence: Then along the hedge we’ll go,
Up and down the garden walk:

readings.title: The Autumn Nosegay
readings.challenge: Notice what autumn takes away and what it still gives.
readings.focus: On a foggy autumn morning, a few late flowers still make a posy among the fallen leaves.
readings.context: A nosegay or posy is a small bunch of flowers. “Sweet” here is a loving name for the child. The naked bough is a bare branch; darksome means dark. The autumn daisy is a small blue or purple daisy that blooms late; lavender has sweet-smelling purple flowers; golden rod is a tall plant with yellow flowers.

excerpt.locator: “The Autumn Nosegay,” the complete poem; opens “Now the fog has risen high, Through the chilly morning air; And the blue and cheerful sky…”; closes “…Shooting up his yellow spear; These are all that we can find, In our posy gay to bind.”.

questions.prompt: What is the weather like on this autumn morning?
facilitatorNotes: Foggy and chilly, with blue sky peeping through here and there.
evidence: Now the fog has risen high,
Through the chilly morning air;

questions.prompt: What has happened to the leaves?
facilitatorNotes: They have turned yellow and fallen from the bare branches all over the garden.
evidence: Ah! the yellow leaves are now
Scatter’d from the naked bough

questions.prompt: Which flowers can they still find? Why so few?
facilitatorNotes: Only the autumn daisy, the lavender and the golden rod; most flowers have faded in the cold. Children may say the posy is small but still pretty.
evidence: Shows its purple blossoms near;
These are all that we can find,

readings.title: The little Ants
readings.challenge: Compare two neighbours and the lesson the poem draws from them.
readings.focus: One ant refuses to help and one helps gladly, and the poem asks children to be like the kind one.
readings.context: A grain of wheat is a seed of the plant bread is made from. “Shift for yourself” means look after yourself; “in want” means needing help; good-natured means kind; endeavour means try; to profit by a story is to learn from it. The last two verses speak to children, not to ants.

excerpt.locator: “The little Ants,” the complete poem; opens “A little black ant found a large grain of wheat, Too heavy to lift or to roll; So he…”; closes “…That if little insects are kind to each other, Then children most certainly ought.”.

questions.prompt: What problem does the first little ant have?
facilitatorNotes: He has found a grain of wheat too heavy to lift or roll into his hole.
evidence: A little black ant found a large grain of wheat,
Too heavy to lift or to roll;

questions.prompt: What does the neighbour do when asked for help, and what does the brother do?
facilitatorNotes: The neighbour says he has his own work and crawls off, cross, to sleep; the brother comes up and helps carry the load in.
evidence: You must shift for yourself, if you please;
Came up and assisted him in with his load;

questions.prompt: What lesson do the last two verses give? Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: If little insects can be kind to each other, children certainly should be; and children are sometimes as cross as the selfish ant. Children may agree, or say that sometimes you really are too busy; ask what the selfish ant could have said instead.
evidence: As cross as the ant, ev’ry bit.
Then children most certainly ought.

readings.title: A Wasp and a Bee
readings.challenge: Follow a conversation and the lesson drawn from it at the end.
readings.focus: A handsome wasp asks why people prefer the plain bee, and the bee says the trouble is the wasp’s sting.
readings.context: Wasps and bees are both striped insects that can sting, and bees make honey. Elegant means graceful; homely means plain; ill-natured means unkind; fair means good-looking. The last verse speaks to people, not to insects.

excerpt.locator: “A Wasp and a Bee,” the complete poem (the initials printed after it omitted); opens “A wasp met a bee that was just buzzing by, And he said, little cousin, can you tell me…”; closes “…the wasp, if ill-natured they are, They will never be loved, if they’re ever so fair.”.

questions.prompt: What is the wasp proud of?
facilitatorNotes: Its shining gold-yellow back and its elegant shape.
evidence: My back shines as bright and as yellow as gold,

questions.prompt: Why does the bee say people do not love the wasp?
facilitatorNotes: Because of its sting and the mischief it does, not because of its looks.
evidence: They cannot put up with, and that is your sting.

questions.prompt: The last verse turns the story into a lesson for people. What is the lesson?
facilitatorNotes: Unkind people will not be loved however good-looking they are: kindness matters more than looks. Some children will point out that bees can sting too, a fair point the poem does not answer.
evidence: Because, like the wasp, if ill-natured they are,
They will never be loved, if they’re ever so fair.
